title: Actor-based session isolation and scaling — RFC review notes
body:
Meeting: Actor-based session isolation and scaling — RFC review
Date: 2024-10-18 11:00-12:00 PT
Location: Zoom + #eng-serving-runtime
Facilitator: Maya Alvarez
Note taker: Benji Chen
Attendees: Maya Alvarez, Benji Chen, Priya Nair, Lucas O'Connor, Anika Singh, Ravi Patel, Zoe Kim (observability)

Purpose
- Review the RFC proposing an actor abstraction for conversation/session isolation (lightweight per-session actors that hold KV pointers, policy metadata, and lifecycle).
- Surface risks, performance tradeoffs, operational impacts, and rollout strategy.

TL;DR decisions from this sync
- Approve RFC in principle with two major constraints: (a) actor heap must be bounded by configurable soft/hard budgets per node; (b) actors opt-in per route via model annotation (no global default).
- Implement a staged rollout: simulation -> e2e load test (staging) -> canary on small percentage of requests -> full rollout behind rollout-policy flag.
- Short-term implementation: an in-process actor registry with eviction hooks integrated with existing KV prefix caching. Long-term: evaluate cross-node actor migration and persistent actor metadata store (optional).

Background/context
- Current model: session affinity binds requests to long-lived runtime workers (session-affinity pins). This works but has limits: poor packing for hundreds of low-activity sessions, memory fragmentation for embeddings/KV caches, and suboptimal GPU utilization during idling sessions. The actor proposal aims to provide a finer-grained lifecycle tied to active request windows while keeping KV cache access low-latency for hot prefixes.

Notes from discussion
1) Actor lifecycle and memory accounting
   - Actor creation: triggered on first request with route annotation; lightweight descriptor allocated in node-local registry.
   - Memory budget: two levels — soft budget triggers LRU-like shrink; hard budget rejects new actor creation and falls back to stateless routing. Configurable at node and tenant level.
   - Eviction policy: prefer actors with zero recent requests and smallest KV footprints. Evicted actors persist metadata to ephemeral actor store for quick rehydrate for 30s before full eviction (to avoid thrash).
   - Garbage collection: run periodic compaction for actor-local caches; expose metrics (actor_count, avg_actor_mem, actor_evictions/sec).

2) Interaction with KV prefix cache and batching
   - KV prefix cache remains shared per-node; actors hold pointers to prefixes rather than full copies to reduce duplication.
   - Batching: continuous batching engine must maintain actor boundaries — cannot mix tokens from different actors in same micro-batch unless same model variant and same actor affinity. Proposal: allow co-batching only when actor isolation policy == relaxed (opt-in) and request metadata marks it safe.
   - Implication: strict isolation reduces batch utilization. Need heuristics to aggregate small-actor requests without violating privacy/consistency (e.g., grouping by tenant + model + safety flags).

3) Routing and rollback behavior
   - Initial routing mode: actor-local (prefer node hosting actor), fallback mode: shard-based routing (stateless) with request replay to cache warm nodes when actor not present.
   - Rollback: add automatic fallback to current session-affinity pins if actor creation fails or node is overloaded. This gives graceful degradation instead of request failures.

4) Performance & cost tradeoffs
   - Pros: lower cold-start latency for active sessions, better tail-latency isolation (no noisy neighbors inside same worker), easier per-session QoS controls.
   - Cons: potential memory overhead and lower batching efficiency for high-cardinality low-throughput sessions. Need to quantify at scale.
   - Simulation results (summary of sandbox run): actor registry + pointerized KV reduced duplicate KV memory by ~35% on synthetic 10k-session workload, but batching utilization dropped 8–12% when strict isolation enforced. (See linked simulation artifacts in GitHub repo.)

5) Safety, multi-tenant, and access controls
   - Actors must inherit tenant auth context and KMS bindings; any actor-local secrets are ephemeral and zeroized on eviction.
   - For enterprise customers on Private deployments we will expose actor memory caps per-tenant and an audit log stream for actor lifecycle events.

6) Observability and SLOs
   - New metrics to add: actor_create_latency_ms, actor_eviction_reason{oom,idle,policy}, actor_rehydrate_latency, actor_eviction_retries, actor_batch_utilization_ratio.
   - Alerts: actor_eviction_rate > 5% sustained for 5m => page (possible memory misconfiguration); avg_actor_mem > soft_budget*1.2 => run autoscaler suggestions.

Alternatives considered (brief)
- Keep session-affinity and improve packing heuristics: low dev cost but limited long-term flexibility.
- Per-tenant worker pools: simpler isolation but poor elasticity and more operational overhead for many tenants.
- Cross-node sticky actor metadata (global actor directory): solves migration but adds complexity and consensus protocols; defer to future phase.

Decisions and rationale
- Proceed with node-local actor registry (phase 1): balances implementation complexity and measurable gains.
- Keep strict actor isolation opt-in per route: avoids surprising behavior for existing routes and lets product owners opt in after validating costs.
- Require default soft/hard budgets to prevent memory amplification across the fleet.

Rollout plan (phased)
1) Simulation & microbench (today -> +2w): refine eviction heuristics, run varying cardinality workloads. Owner: Priya (due 2024-10-25).
2) Staging e2e load tests (2–3w): integrate with KV cache and batching engine, observe batch utilization and tail-latency. Owner: Lucas (due 2024-11-08).
3) Canary (1% traffic, 1 region) (after successful staging): monitor actor metrics and eviction rates. Owner: Anika (due 2024-11-22).
4) Gradual ramp with rollout-policy flag and guard rails (2–6w). Owner: Maya & SRE (due 2024-12-06).

Action items (explicit)
- Priya: extend simulator to include mixed micro-batch workloads and actor opt-in flags. Attach simulation scripts to PR. (due 2024-10-25)
- Lucas: prototype in-process registry and a simple eviction hook with KV pointer semantics; open draft PR for review. (due 2024-11-01)
- Benji: add observability requirements to metrics pipeline + dashboards mockups; coordinate with Zoe for alert thresholds. (due 2024-10-28)
- Anika: define canary experiment plan (traffic split, rollback criteria, success criteria). (due 2024-11-15)
- Ravi: enumerate security implications for enterprise private deployments (KMS, audit logs) and draft a compliance checklist. (due 2024-10-30)

Open questions / unknowns
- How often will active actor churn occur in real workloads (not synthetic)? Need production trace sampling.
- Is cross-node actor migration necessary for meaningful ROI? Might be required for long-running sessions that move between regions.
- Precise memory accounting for pointerized KV vs small local cache — edge cases where pointer indirection increases lookup latency.

Notes to reviewers
- The RFC branch contains simulation artifacts and a small harness for replaying production-like traces. Please run the harness with your route traces where possible and paste observations in the PR comments.
- We specifically opted not to change the batching engine contract yet; the first iteration preserves per-actor batching boundaries and exposes flags to relax if product owner accepts throughput cost.

Appendix (quick links)
- Simulation results: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/sim/actor-sim/results-20241017.csv
- Draft RFC: confluence:Serving Runtime > Actor Model RFC (draft)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2187

End of notes.
summary: Notes from RFC review for actor-based session isolation. Approved in principle with memory caps and opt-in policy. Staged rollout and a set of actionable owners/dates defined. Several simulation results summarized and follow-up tasks assigned.
